title: Syllables, word parts, definition, then example
statement: Teach a new multi-syllable word in a fixed order: hear it in syllables, break it into meaningful parts where it has them, give its definition, then an example.
detail: A ruling for a Grade 3 reading course extended an earlier rule that put syllables before word parts into a fixed four-step sequence for every taught word: syllable highlighting so the child hears how the word is spoken, then the word-part breakdown that unlocks meaning, then the definition, then an example. Syllables are spoken parts and word parts are meaningful elements, so the split into word parts is a separate, later move, taught as a strategy for deriving meaning only where a word breaks into meaningful parts. It is a course ruling, and no outcome was measured.

evidence.quote: the full instruction sequence for a vocabulary word is syllable highlighting (hear how the word is spoken) → morpheme breakdown (unlock meaning) → definition → example, in that order
this confirms and extends R-VOC-14a (which already ordered syllables before morphemes) by fixing the full four-step sequence
the morpheme split is a separate, later move.
"Morphemes are meaningful elements, syllables are spoken parts" — the two must never be conflated on one tile.
where a word breaks into meaningful parts, teach the split as a strategy for deriving meaning
